title: Enhanced Long-Wavelength Fluctuations and Interaction-Stress Correlations in Active Crystals
abstract: Activity can enhance the long-wavelength density fluctuations of a solid beyond the equilibrium fluctuations predicted by the Mermin-Wagner-Hohenberg theorem, but the microscopic origin of this enhancement remains unclear. We study a two-dimensional active Brownian crystal whose longitudinal and transverse displacement covariances scale as $C^u_λ(q)\sim q^{-3}$ as compared to the passive counterpart with $q^{-2}$ law. This spectrum predicts an MSD-plateau divergence proportional to $L$ in two dimensions, logarithmic in three dimensions, and finite in four dimensions, in close correspondence with recent results reported in Dey et al. [Nat. Commun. 16, 5498 (2025)]. Inverse of the Covariance gives $H^{\mathrm{cov}}_λ\sim |q|^3$ with the corresponding dispersion $ω_{\mathrm{cov},λ}\sim q^{3/2}$, whereas direct mechanical response gives $K_{\mathrm{resp},λ}\sim q^2$ and acoustic modes with $ω_{0,λ}\sim q$. The nonlinear dispersion is therefore covariance-defined rather than mechanical. The mobility and integrated active-force correlations remain non-singular, although a finite-persistence crossover cannot be ruled out completely with the existing data. Microscopically, the longitudinal and transverse Irving-Kirkwood interaction-stress spectra scale as $q^{-1}$. The transverse stress-stress correlation connects well with the anomalous displacement field, indicating that activity anomalously populates ordinary acoustic modes, while the conservative interaction network transmits the resulting fluctuations as long-ranged stress. A three-dimensional active FCC crystal exhibits the same paired low-$q$ trends.
summary: This work analyzes how activity fundamentally alters the long-wavelength fluctuations in crystalline solids, showing that the enhancement scales as $q^{-3}$ rather than the expected $q^{-2}$. The authors demonstrate that this anomaly originates from long-range stress correlations induced by the active forces, providing a key theoretical insight into non-equilibrium solid physics.
main_problem: The paper investigates the microscopic origin of enhanced long-wavelength density fluctuations in active solids, which violate equilibrium predictions like the Mermin-Wagner-Hohenberg theorem.
main_result: Activity enhances long-wavelength fluctuations, causing the displacement covariance to scale anomalously as $q^{-3}$ (instead of $q^{-2}$), and this anomaly is traced to long-range stress correlations rather than mechanical softening.
method: The study uses theoretical analysis of active Brownian motion, calculating displacement covariances, response stiffness, and interaction-stress spectra in Fourier space.
model_or_system: The system modeled is a two-dimensional active Brownian crystal, governed by equations of motion incorporating conservative pair forces and active propulsion forces.
key_observables: Displacement covariance ($\langle |u_\lambda(q)|^2 angle$), interaction-stress spectra ($S_{	ext{stress}}(q)$), and the resulting Mean Squared Displacement (MSD) scaling.
important_parameters: Propulsion strength ($f_0$), wavevector ($q$), and dimensionality (2D and 3D).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on decomposing the covariance and comparing it against predictions from linear elasticity and equilibrium fluctuation theories.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the $q^{-3}$ enhancement of displacement and stress spectra in active crystals compared to passive ones, and show the scaling of the MSD with system size L.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the anomalous scaling of the displacement covariance ($q^{-3}$ vs $q^{-2}$), then ruling out nonlocal elastic softening by comparing it to the measured response stiffness ($q^2$), and finally attributing the anomaly to the structure of non-equilibrium stress fluctuations.
why_interesting: While focused on classical active matter, the methodology of analyzing non-equilibrium fluctuations and deviations from equilibrium theorems (like MWH) is highly relevant to understanding open quantum systems and dissipation in quantum many-body dynamics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Activity-enhanced displacement fluctuations in the two-dimensional crystal. (a) Transverse displacement covariance Cu T (q) = ⟨|uT (q)|2⟩and (b) longitudinal displacement covariance Cu L(q) = ⟨|uL(q)|2⟩for the indicated propulsion strengths f0. The passive spectra are consistent with the conventional elastic scaling Cu λ(q) ∼q−2. Increasing activity selectively enhances the long-wavelength modes. At low-q, the transverse spectrum approaches the q−3 guide, whereas the longitudinal spectrum displays a weaker effective dependence, approximately q−2.5.

FIG. 2. (a) Static response stiffness Kresp,λ(q) = χ−1 λ (q) for the longitudinal and transverse polarizations. Different open symbols denote the probe amplitudes A = 5 × 10−4, 10−3, and 2 × 10−3 and f0 = 2.0. Their collapse demonstrates that the probe lies within the linear-response regime. Both polarizations exhibit the ordinary elastic scaling Kresp,λ(q) ∼q2, rather than the |q|3 behavior inferred from covariance inversion. The dashed and dotted lines indicate q2 and q3 guides, respectively. (b) Equal-time mode-dependent fluctuation–response ratio Tmode,λ(q) = Kresp,λ(q)Cu λ(q) for the longitudinal and transverse polarizations for f0 = 2.0. Both branches increase toward small q,...

Figure 2(b) shows Tmode,λ(q) obtained by combining the measured response kernel with the displacement co- variance for f0 = 2.0. Both polarizations exhibit an en- hancement toward small q, with a substantially larger amplitude in the transverse sector. The transverse data are approximately compatible with a q−1 dependence over the low q regime. The longitudinal data show a weaker increase, and therefore do not establish a clean inverse-q scaling. At larger q, both polarizations ap- proach the thermal background scale, Tmode,λ ≃kBT, indicating that the nonequilibrium enhancement is con- centrated predominantly in the long-wavelength modes.

FIG. 3. Tests of nonlocal kinetic mechanisms. (a,b) Normalised response Rλ(q, t) for different low-q transverse and longitudinal modes, respectively, at activity strength f0 = 2.0. (c) Wave-vector-dependent mobility Mλ(q) = 1/ζλ(q) obtained from the dynamic response. Both longitudinal and transverse mobilities remain approximately constant, consistent with the q0 guide and inconsistent with the singular Mλ ∼q−1 behavior for f0 = 2.0. (d) Dynamic stiffness Kλ fitted from the response function.

FIG. 4. Normalised gλ correlation for (a) transverse and (b) longitudinal modes as a function of time for different low-q values at activity strength f0 = 2.0. (c) Correlation time τ f λ (q) of the bare active-force modes for different propulsion strengths. The longitudinal and transverse results remain close to the single-particle persistence time D−1 r and do not follow the q−1 guide. (c) Correlation time τ g λ(q) of the effective residual force gλ = f a λ + (f int λ −f harm λ ). Insets: integrated autocorrelation intensities, Dλ(q), for active and residual force with activity strength f0 = 2.0 for longitudinal and transverse modes.
